title: Google Home update fixes Nest ‘Live View’ issues, improves Nest Hub and Gemini for speakers
snippet: A new Google Home update is rolling out with a fix for “Live View” issues affecting Nest Cam devices, improvements for the Nest Hub, upgrades for Gemini, and more. more…
fullText:
A new Google Home update is rolling out with a fix for “Live View” issues affecting Nest Cam devices, improvements for the Nest Hub, upgrades for Gemini, and more.

As per usual, the latest Google Home update can be split up into a few categories, starting with Gemini. Still in early access, enrolled users can expect further improvements to smart home controls, faster timers, and “more conversational voice feedback,” as well as faster Broadcasts.

Most notable on the Gemini front is improvements to Nest Hubs, with smart displays now showing “relevant images when helpful” when you ask questions.

Visual answers with images on smart displays: On-screen answers on smart displays now will include relevant images when helpful so you can take in information at a glance.

In the Google Home app, Google is adding a “Google Home Premium” page to the settings menu, an “Eco Mode Everywhere” toggle for homes with multiple Nest Thermostats, and support for Home keys in Google Wallet for compatible locks.

	

Google Wallet rolling out digital Google Home keys with supported locks on Android

More software updates are rolling out for older Nest Cam devices, including a fix for the “Live View” issue that’s been in place on some devices such as Nest Hello. You can also remove an unmigrated Nest Hello from the Home app even if it is offline. Other camera updates in this update include:

More reliable camera history player controls (Android): Fixed issues in camera event history where the previous and next event buttons or player controls could be missing or unresponsive on still-image events, timeline gaps, or playback error screens, or get stuck loading when rotating your phone.

Fewer unnecessary Nest account linking prompts (Android): Fixed an issue where already-linked users could be prompted with “Do you have a Nest account?” during brief network interruptions.

Clearer account relinking for partner cameras (Android): Fixed an issue where third-party cameras with an expired partner account link appeared offline instead of showing the option to relink your account.

Offline legacy Nest Doorbell removal (Android): Restored the option in device settings to remove an offline unmigrated Nest Doorbell (wired, 1st gen).

Software updates for Nest Cam Indoor (1st gen), Nest Cam Outdoor (1st gen), Nest Doorbell (wired, 1st gen / Nest Hello), Nest Cam IQ Indoor, and Nest Cam IQ Outdoor migrated to the Google Home app:

Fixed live streaming connection issues on certain network connections: Resolved an issue where live streaming could fail to connect over certain internet connections (such as PPPoE, fiber, or mobile hotspots) while event history continued recording normally, and improved live stream responsiveness and smoothness.

Restored event thumbnails on Nest Cam IQ: Fixed an issue on Nest Cam IQ Indoor and Nest Cam IQ Outdoor where event previews in the Google Home app could appear blank.

Improved playback timestamps and camera reliability: Improved camera clock accuracy for reliable event history timestamps, updated security certificates, and fixed stability issues to reduce unexpected camera restarts.

On the AI agent front, Google Home MCP connections now allow agents to control automations as well as accessing new controls and status checks across “thermostats, fans, air purifiers, robot vacuums, lighting effects, kitchen appliances, EV chargers, and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.”

Google is also rolling out smart speaker updates right now, but details on what’s new are limited.

title: Google Pixel rolls out new ‘Family Hub’ feature with useful controls [Gallery]
snippet: First appearing earlier this month, Google Pixel phones are rolling out a handy new Family feature in the Settings menu. Here’s what it can do. more…
fullText:
First appearing earlier this month, Google Pixel phones are rolling out a handy new Family feature in the Settings menu. Here’s what it can do.

Rolling out now via what appears to be a server-side update (tied to Google Play Services), Google Pixel phones are adding a “Family” section to the Settings menu. The feature is appearing for us on a Pixel 11 Pro XL running the October 2026 update (not Android 17 QPR2), while a Pixel 10 Pro has also just surfaced the new UI.

This new section, which Google has previously referred to as “Family Hub,” gives users a quick place to see their family members and settings in one central location. It shows a list of your family members – child accounts and anyone attached to your Google One family plan – with controls over Google One storage, Google Play Family Library, shared payment methods, and “Family events” in Google Calendar.

You can also see the live location of any family members you are sharing your location with or start sharing your location with another family member. You can also easily remove or add members to your family plan via this new menu. Each family member gets their own page where you can see benefits shared, location, and also if they are a “parent” in the family – with “remove” and “transfer” options available.

	

	

While this won’t be helpful for all users, it’s certainly full of useful shortcuts and tools for those at the center of a family plan and looking to share benefits with their household. 

As far as we can tell, this is widely rolled out to Pixel owners at this point. As mentioned, we’re seeing it across multiple devices, and 9to5Google readers mentioned they’re also seeing it live even prior to installing the latest system update. The folks at Droid-Life also mention now seeing it on their Pixels.

title: Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding
snippet: Science Corp. raised a $400 million Series D to scale up its anti-blindness business.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

6:26 AM PST · November 17, 2026

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

		

							

											
									

					

	

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company said in a blog post.

Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.

Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

title: iPhone Duo Gets a Facial Unlock Feature, but It’s Not Face ID. What to Know
snippet: Unlocking Apple’s foldable should get a lot easier, but there are some caveats.
fullText:
One of the iPhone Duo‘s biggest drawbacks has just been addressed – mostly. 

Unlike Apple’s other current iPhones, the iPhone Duo lacks Face ID, meaning you have to rely on the noticeably less speedy Touch ID or enter a passcode to unlock the foldable device. This would be less painful if the Duo didn’t cost $1,999, and if Face ID hadn’t long been a standard feature across the company’s other iPhones, including its most affordable option. 

Now, there’s something of a fix. In its latest iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple has added an option to unlock the iPhone Duo using the front camera. This should make accessing the phone’s contents more seamless and intuitive. 

		

			

Until now, my least favorite aspect of using the iPhone Duo has been the inability to unlock using facial recognition – a limitation that stands in stark contrast to the foldable phone’s premium feel. Scanning a fingerprint with Touch ID not only feels antiquated for such a pricey device, but also rather slow. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, by contrast, has a facial recognition feature, as well as fingerprint unlocking that’s much faster than the Duo’s.

It appears Apple heard our cries and is bringing a workaround to the Duo. This new unlocking capability isn’t quite the same as Face ID, a more secure biometric facial recognition and authentication system. Instead, the iPhone Duo will now let you unlock the phone using the selfie camera under slightly more limited conditions to help ensure security.

Read more: Meet the Custom-Built Machine That Has Folded the iPhone Duo 500,000 Times

How to unlock the iPhone Duo using the front camera

To enable the new optional unlock feature, go to your Duo’s Settings and toggle it on under Touch ID & Passcode. Because unlocking with the Duo’s front camera isn’t as secure as using Touch ID or Face ID, you’ll need to use Touch ID or enter a passcode after around 45 minutes of inactivity. Touch ID is also required when using Apple Pay or accessing your passwords.

Unlocking with the front camera is possible because of a new capability in Apple silicon called Secure Exclaves. The iPhone Duo uses this to securely and privately process data of a user’s face and verify the match. That means iOS, apps, users and Apple can’t access the data used to unlock the phone via the front camera. 

I admittedly didn’t think this update would arrive on Apple’s first-generation foldable; I assumed we’d just have to cross our fingers and hope for Face ID to land on the next iteration. It’s a relatively small improvement, but one that I think will make the Duo experience a lot more convenient and in line with the phone’s modern design and aesthetics, even if it’s not a full Face ID fix. As much as I thought I could make do with Touch ID, it turned out to be more of a nuisance than I’d anticipated; I’m so used to the speediness of unlocking by simply looking at a phone’s screen and swiping up. So I’m glad there’s a software update to help address that gap on the Duo. 

The next iOS 27.3 developer beta also adds the option for the iPhone Duo to automatically lock when someone closes the phone. You can enable this under Settings > Display & Brightness. 

Alongside other recent software updates, including the addition of Reachability to make the Duo’s cover screen content easier to access one-handed, and support for Apple Pencil with USB-C, Apple appears poised to continue rolling out features that make the Duo more adaptable.

title: MagSafe Monday: MOFT’s Trackable Field Wallet holds eight cards, cash, and supports Find My
snippet: The one thing Apple’s own MagSafe wallet does that a few third-party wallets have is Find My. If you misplace your wallet, your iPhone tells you where it is. Most MagSafe wallets either skip tracking entirely or have a pocket for an AirTag, which adds thickness and it’s another thing to buy. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet builds the tracker into the wallet itself, so it shows up in the Find My app. more…
fullText:
The one thing Apple’s own MagSafe wallet does that a few third-party wallets have is Find My. If you misplace your wallet, your iPhone tells you where it is. Most MagSafe wallets either skip tracking entirely or have a pocket for an AirTag, which adds thickness and it’s another thing to buy. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet builds the tracker into the wallet itself, so it shows up in the Find My app.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

MOFT has been making the origami-style folding wallet for many years, and this model works like any other Find My accessory. So that means you get left-behind alerts when you leave without it, and the ability to make it trackable through Apple’s network if it’s across town instead of under the couch. It also works with Google’s Find Hub on Android, which matters if you’ve got a mixed household of devices.

The wallet is powered by a built-in battery rather than a watch-style battery, and MOFT says a charge lasts about six months. You charge it by placing the wallet on a Qi charger for about an hour and a half, which, in practice, means dropping it on a MagSafe dock twice a year. That’s a better setup than an AirTag in a wallet as well.

MOFT Trackable Field Wallet capacity and stand

The wallet holds up to eight cards, or closer to four to six if you also use the hidden compartment for cash. A pull tab in the wallet brings your everyday cards out in one motion, while your driver’s license and cash stay tucked inside of it. It’s made from MOFT’s vegan leather and at 14 mm thick, it’s slimmer than a traditional wallet but noticeably thicker than Apple’s card-only wallet, which is the price you are going to pay to hold up this much stuff.

The stand is the usual MOFT origami fold-out, and it works in portrait and landscape for FaceTime or watching a video on the plane. You can buy it without the stand if you’d rather have the thinner version. It comes in Jet Black, Misty Cove, Terracotta, and Peony.

Two things to know going in. There’s no RFID blocking in this version (MOFT has a non-Find My Snap Field Wallet if you want that). MOFT also warns that the magnets can affect magnetic-stripe cards, so avoid putting a hotel key in it.

Wrap up on MOFT Trackable Field Wallet

I’ve spent the past month on a Pelican accessory beat, using wallets designed for outdoor use. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is the other end of that accessory spectrum: more cards, a stand, and Find My built in. If Find My is the reason you’ve stuck with Apple’s wallet, this is a really nice option that holds a bunch and is trackable.

The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is available on Amazon and directly from MOFT.

title: Samsung Galaxy’s next major update keeps leaking – here’s what to expect in One UI 9.5
snippet: Samsung is preparing its next major update for Galaxy phones, One UI 9.5, and new details have been coming to light. Here’s an overview of a lot of One UI 9.5 updates that have leaked so far. more…
fullText:
Samsung is preparing its next major update for Galaxy phones, One UI 9.5, and new details have been coming to light. Here’s an overview of a lot of One UI 9.5 updates that have leaked so far.

One UI 9.5 will still be based on Android 17, but it’s set to be packed with various changes based on recent leaks. In particular, it seems like Samsung has a ton of new AI features in store.

“Galaxy Claw” is supposedly Samsung’s new “personal agent,” able to leverage apps on your device including your notifications, Contacts, Gmail, Messages, and more. Specifically, Android Authority reports it will be able to use Calendar, Contacts, Gallery, Gmail, Messages, Notifications, Perplexity, Phone, and Voice Recorder, with the agent able to set up scheduled tasks. It does sound like this will be a paid feature, though, with Samsung’s new $4.99/month AI Premium plan. There would also be a new dashboard for showing AI usage.

There’s also a new Memory feature in Bixby that would let the assistant reference past details from conversations or commands. 

	

Daily Brief, sharing its name with Google’s canceled Pixel feature, would be able to summarize notifications from various apps, grouping cards into “Finance and payments,” “Bookings and appointments,” and “Work email,” though that list seems incomplete. 

It’s not all about AI. It also looks like Samsung’s Expert RAW camera experience is being improved with better labels, customizable buttons, a screen lock option, burst mode support, and more. It even seems like there’s video support coming.

Other new features that have leaked include:

Custom greetings in Call Screening

“Meal Scan” for calorie counts/macros based on photos

Contact widgets with AI-powered call summaries, replies, etc

Tap to Share (already available on Pixel)

Search button in the Phone app

Birthday section in Samsung’s Contacts app

Rambler-like voice-to-text in Samsung Keyboard

“Play-on” integrates notifications and messages from games into Now Brief, more

One UI 9.5 will almost certainly be launching on next year’s Galaxy S27 series before expanding to more devices later on, as has been the case for the past several updates. A beta program will likely be available on Galaxy S26 series soon – the One UI 8.5 beta program opened up in early December 2025.

title: Samsung’s ‘Galaxy Studio’ headphones leak with touch controls, two colors
snippet: We’re only a couple of months away from our next Galaxy Unpacked, and while the expanded Galaxy S27 series is practically guaranteed to show up, the real fun tends to lie in whatever other gadgets show up alongside Samsung’s next flagship smartphone release. Based on some new leaks, it’s sure looking like the next mobile accessory on the company’s docket is a return to over-ear wireless headphones, and so far, they’re sounding pretty promising. more…
fullText:
We’re only a couple of months away from our next Galaxy Unpacked, and while the expanded Galaxy S27 series is practically guaranteed to show up, the real fun tends to lie in whatever other gadgets show up alongside Samsung’s next flagship smartphone release. Based on some new leaks, it’s sure looking like the next mobile accessory on the company’s docket is a return to over-ear wireless headphones, and so far, they’re sounding pretty promising.

Samsung hasn’t produced over-ear headphones in about a decade — under its own name, at least — but it looks like that’s about to change. We hadn’t heard much in the way of details on the company’s next audio release, rumored to be named ‘Galaxy Studio,’ but a fresh leak courtesy of SamMobile is finally changing that. We’ll have to keep waiting for full renders, but these leaked graphics are giving us a general idea of what they might look like, plus a couple of key features.

Unsurprisingly, Galaxy Studio will include ANC, complete with a dedicated button to toggle the setting between its usual modes. Volume controls also could come in the shape of physical buttons, but playback controls appear to be relegated to a touch-sensitive area on its earpads, something that’s become relatively standard among the flagship headphone competition. SamMobile also reports it’ll come in “at least” black and red colorways, while a leak from earlier this month suggested rotational earcups.

Okay, is it me or is the random goatee in this graphic crazy?

Again, I don’t want to read too much into these leaked graphics, as it’s always possible the final release has a handful of changes. title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO
snippet: In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signalled his willingness to return as CEO.
fullText:
In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signalled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest. 

Huang’s statement, posted in full on X, reads as follows:

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. 

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. 

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1.

In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.

Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick.

“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.”

Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told the Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms. 

Reached by Politico, one senator called Huang’s reinstatement “one of the worst ideas I’ve heard today.”

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

After first announcing its Flipper One last May, which the company describes as an “open Linux multi-tool built for high-performance computing and IP networking,” Flipper Devices has launched a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign where you can preorder the device for $399 with shipping expected to start in July 2027.

The Flipper One is more expensive than the company’s popular but controversial Flipper Zero wireless hacking multitool, which is currently available for $169. However, Flipper Devices points out that the new Flipper One isn’t a successor to the Flipper Zero, but a completely different product.

While the Zero’s capabilities focused on NFC, RFID, infrared, and Sub-1GHz wireless frequencies, the much larger Flipper One offers expanded connectivity with two gigabit ethernet ports, PCIe, SATA, and USB 3.0 interfaces, and Wi-Fi 6e support. There’s also an M.2 slot for connecting modules that include a 5G modem and a mesh networking LoRa radio that can turn the Flipper One into a walkie-talkie.

It’s still pocket-friendly, but the Flipper One is powered by an 8-core RK3576 ARM processor with a dedicated NPU and a GPU that supports connectivity to an external display over USB-C or HDMI. Flipper Devices suggests the One can be used as everything from a networking diagnostics tool to a media player when connected to a TV. It runs Flipper OS, which is based on Debian Linux and features an open source firmware so that users can develop their own apps, tools, and uses for the device.

title: New camera sensor coming to the iPhone 20 Pro’s main camera, says leaker
snippet: The biggest improvement to iPhone photo quality that Apple could make would be to give the device a larger sensor. There have been two reports suggesting this is on the way, although with a potentially rather large catch. A leaker today says that the iPhone 20 Pro is getting a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera, but details are unclear … more…
fullText:
The biggest improvement to iPhone photo quality that Apple could make would be to give the device a larger sensor. There have been two reports suggesting this is on the way, although with a potentially rather large catch.

A leaker today says that the iPhone 20 Pro is getting a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera, but details are unclear …

There are two main reasons people still buy standalone cameras despite having an iPhone in their pocket wherever they go. The first is lens quality: iPhones have small plastic lenses compared to the far larger and more sophisticated glass lenses used with dedicated cameras.

The second is sensor size. All other things being equal, a larger sensor will capture more light and provide a higher quality image. Current smartphone sensors are absolutely tiny compared to those used in even mid-range consumer cameras.

Larger sensor on the way

We’ve seen two previous reports suggesting that a larger sensor is on the way for future iPhones. One of these suggested that it would be coming in 2027 or 2028, although a later one suggested the latter date was more likely.

The reports were not without a catch, however, suggesting that the larger sensor would only be for the telephoto lens and would have a 200MP resolution. Squeezing more pixels into a given sensor size tends to sacrifice low light capabilities in return for higher resolution. This is less likely to be an issue with a telephoto lens, which is normally used outdoors rather than inside.

What I’d really love to see is a significantly larger sensor for the main camera, with no increase in resolution. This would improve low light performance and overall image quality.

New sensor for the iPhone 20 Pro

A brief report from leaker Ice Universe suggests that the iPhone 20 Pro will get a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera.

iPhone 20 Pro to feature a new sensor using 17nm logic process for its main camera next year.

(Under Apple’s current naming system, next year’s iPhone Pro would be the iPhone 19 Pro. However, it’s widely expected that Apple will jump to the iPhone 20 nomenclature in order to mark a significant design upgrade for the 20th anniversary of the device.)

There are no further details, so we don’t know whether the size of the sensor will be increased or remain the same.

title: Nintendo will soon discontinue Google and Apple sign-ins
snippet: Nintendo Switch users have until January 25 to change how they sign in to the Nintendo Switch app on their smartphones. more…
fullText:
Nintendo Switch users have until January 25 to change how they sign in to the Nintendo Switch app on their smartphones.

Nintendo is going all-in on passkeys in a scheduled update to the Nintendo Switch app and will be sunsetting 3rd party logins after January 25, 2027. The news was made available on an official Nintendo support page. That means you won’t be able to use your Google or Apple accounts to log in to your Nintendo account as of January 26. After January 26:

You cannot use your Google or Apple accounts to log in to your Nintendo Account.

You cannot create a new Nintendo Account using a Google or Apple account.

The My Nintendo Platinum Points mission to link your Google account to your Nintendo Account is also discontinued.

Instead of using 3rd-party account linking, Nintendo is recommending that users register a passkey for an exclusive, secure login experience through the Nintendo Switch app. If you forget to do this before January 26, you can always head to the Nintendo account page and run through the “forgot password” instructions. Nintendo recommends making sure you can log in to your account ASAP via non-Google or Apple links to ensure that you don’t run into problems before January.

Nintendo didn’t elaborate on the policy change, although some surmise it’s based on security-related measures. The advancement of AI has created bots that can hack into systems with unprecedented speed, so it’s possible that Nintendo is simply trying to shore up any possible area it cannot 100% control. Either way, if you use the Nintendo Switch app or have a Nintendo account of any kind, you should change how you log in immediately.

title: This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference
snippet: When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control. But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so … more…
fullText:
When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

For still photography, I have these:

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

title: Wyze’s new door lock has speedy fingerprint recognition and 12-month battery life
snippet: Wyze is today launching its new “Lever Lock,” a smart lock for your front door that has a year of battery life and fast fingerprint recognition, all for an affordable price tag. more…
fullText:
Wyze is today launching its new “Lever Lock,” a smart lock for your front door that has a year of battery life and fast fingerprint recognition, all for an affordable price tag.

Available starting today, the Wyze Level Lock is not your typical deadbolt smart lock. Rather, this is a smart lock designed for your standard single-bore latch, meaning it’s available for doors that other smart locks aren’t compatible with. You can still have a deadbolt, but you’ll need enough space for both (per Wyze’s guidelines below).

The Lever Lock has a PIN entry and a fingerprint sensor, the latter of which Wyze says recognizes your fingerprint in about half a second. It uses local storage for biometric data and works to improve that data with each successful unlock. 

The PIN has a clever feature (though it’s presented in somewhat poor taste) that lets you input random digits before or after your actual code to prevent onlookers from being able to see your code. There’s also a physical key backup as well as a USB-C input on the outside in the case that the battery dies – Wyze says it lasts about 12 months on a charge using eight AA batteries.

	

The Wyze Lever Lock is available today for $99.98 and shipping immediately.

Android XR glasses get their own control wearable, but you might already own it. Google says the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch will be able to control Android XR glasses.

Google just launched its line of Intelligent Eyewear glasses. The smart glasses run on Android XR with hardware built by Samsung. They start at $395, with pre-orders opening up today through both Warby Parker and Gentle Monster.

For all the smart features they have, one of the best might be the sly integration Google is setting up between Intelligent Eyewear and its existing wearables. Google quietly noted that both Pixel Watch models and the Fitbit Air will be able to control Android XR glasses, like a dedicated control band some competitor smart glasses come with.

Pixel Watch already supports gesture controls using sensors to detect movements like finger pinching or wrist adjustments. Google’s Android XR demo included pausing and playing music using a pinch gesture. We imagine gesture controls will support as much as the touchpad that sits in the arms of Intelligent Eyewear models, though it’s not clear what gestures will be supported just yet. You’ll still be able to use the touch sensors, but Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air will be just another avenue. 

	

According to what Google told us, the Pixel Watch will be supported around launch, with Fitbit Air adding support sometime in 2027. Galaxy Watch will also be supported on Samsung devices. Considering the Fitbit Air is reportedly such a massive hit that Google is having a hard time keeping up, the move only makes sense. The Fitbit Air is also only $99, whereas something like Meta’s Neural Band goes for $199.

title: I Didn’t Expect to Like Xiaomi’s Bizarre Dual-Screen Phone So Much
snippet: Review: Xiaomi’s 18 Pro Max is a quirky Android phone that stands out from the crowd with its extra screen on the back. Shame Americans can’t have it.
fullText:
Xiaomi teased me with the 17 Pro, its bizarre dual-screen Android phone, last year. But it was sold only in China. Being from the UK, I went back to my regular boring phone with its boring single screen. Big sigh. So imagine my excitement when Xiaomi announced that its new flagship 18 Pro and Pro Max — complete with a second rear screen — would launch internationally, with a rollout including the UK and wider Europe. As with the rest of Xiaomi’s handsets, people in the US are flat out of luck. 

That sucks for Americans because this phone is actually damn good. I worried that the rear screen would just be a dumb gimmick — something that tries to separate the phone from competitors but doesn’t actually add anything useful. But I actually like it. Need it? No. But it’s fun and has some genuine uses. 

Beyond the screen, though, the 18 Pro Max packs the latest Qualcomm Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, a fast-charging silicon-carbon battery and a potent camera setup that utilizes the same LOFIC sensor technology that impressed me so much in Xiaomi and Leica’s Leitzphone earlier this year. 

			

More from CNET

From the front you wouldn’t know there’s anything unusual about this phone.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The 18 Pro isn’t just smaller (6.4 inches vs. the Pro Max’s 6.9 inches) it misses some of the Max’s top tech as well. The processor is a lesser model, the main camera doesn’t use LOFIC tech and the smaller battery isn’t as capable. Shame.

But the 18 Pro Max is an all-round Android powerhouse, and I’ve really enjoyed getting to grips with it over the past couple of weeks. Here’s what I’ve found and what you need to know about this phone. 

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: What’s with that second screen? 

The extra display on the back is certainly this phone’s standout feature. It’s basically in the same place as the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera island, but instead of just being a piece of metal, it’s an actual functioning screen. If you’ve ever seen the cover display on a clamshell flip phone like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8, then it’ll seem quite familiar. 

Like the Flip 8, the second display shows incoming notifications, acting as a camera viewfinder and offering a variety of basic built-in functions like calendar reminders. What really hooked me, though, was the ability to create Gen AI apps just by typing in a prompt. 

For example, I asked for “a game where you just pop bubbles,” which the “Polish” tool elaborated on with deeper functions and visual styles before generating a finished game that was fully playable on the back screen, complete with a scoring system and, for some reason, a jellyfish mascot. It takes about 5 minutes for the app to be created each time, and its functions are limited. It’s not able to access any app data, so don’t expect to create a new email reader, and anything too technical will result in failure. 

Screenshot by Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I asked it to create a camera overlay that showed exposure settings (shutter speed, ISO and so on) to serve as a light meter for an analog camera. I’m not sure whether the issue was my explanation or a technical limitation, but it took the phone two tries to get something close. It created an interface with dials and exposure information, but it didn’t open the camera to calculate exposure as I’d hoped. As a result, it looked nice but it was functionally redundant.

Another time, I asked it to create an app that showed real-time charging speeds. The resulting app showed current battery level but not charging speed. It did have a baffling “charging milestones completed” button that simply increased by one each time I tapped it. I also had no luck with my “rude word generator,” which just repeatedly came back with “Couldn’t generate.” Frustratingly, each time it fails to create an app, it doesn’t tell you why — like if you’re asking for information it’s unable to access — but just says to try again “in a minute or two,” which rarely resulted in success in my testing time. If I’m asking for something it can’t achieve, it’d be helpful to know that. 

Even so, I’m impressed with this app creation tool and, like many of the AI tools that only mildly excite me right now, I can only assume it will improve over time. 

One of my favorite uses of the rear screen, though, is for vlogging. Firstly, seeing yourself from the back of the phone means you’re able to accurately film yourself using the best quality camera, rather than limiting yourself to the front-facing camera, which won’t look as good. But there’s also an autocue function where you can input a script and have it overlaid as text, allowing you to read out your words as you present to camera.

If you use the rear screen for your selfies, the image quality will be far better than using the front-facing camera.

It’s a powerful tool for vloggers and other video creators who rely on longer prewritten scripts for their videos. But it’s quite basic: the text simply auto-scrolls at a speed you set in advance. I’d love to see Xiaomi use voice recognition here to automatically progress the text as you read out the words, slowing down or speeding up as you naturally read aloud. This tech already exists, so I don’t think I’m asking for literal magic here.

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: Great cameras for creative photographers

Tucked into that second display is a 200-megapixel main camera and a 200-megapixel telephoto camera offering 3.2x optical zoom or 6.4x hybrid zoom. There’s also a really tiny 50-megapixel ultrawide camera by itself below the camera island, which makes it feel like an afterthought — something that I’ll come back to later. 

The main sensor is physically slightly smaller than the one in Xiaomi’s Leitzphone, but it uses the same LOFIC sensor tech for better dynamic range in a single image. I’ve taken a lot of photos with it so far and I’m really impressed with what I’ve seen. The smaller 18 Pro has an almost identical camera setup but its main sensor doesn’t use LOFIC, which is a shame as it forces you to go for the larger phone if you want the best possible image quality.

There are loads of ways to customise the look of your images and I love the warm tones and superb dynamic range of this shot. Andrew Lanxon/CNET
Pin sharp focusing on the flower, great colors and perfect exposure. No notes.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
It’s a relatively low-light shot, but this image is sharp, noise-free and has great colors.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Shots are well-exposed, with accurate colors and fine details that manage to look sharp but without the harsh over-sharpened look that’s all too often seen from phone cameras. Images look more natural as a result. 

I like the standard look (left) and while the oranges are a bit much in the filmic look version (right) I do like how much it leans into those fall vibes.

There are a lot of ways to tune your images in-camera — almost too many, in fact. There’s a whole host of built-in color presets, including a Leica-branded high-contrast black-and-white mode that I like, all of which you can customize further by adjusting the tones, colors, grain and white balance. Then there’s the option to shoot using the phone’s default color processing, going with “Leica Vibrant” for more popping colors or “Leica Authentic” for more natural tones. Each of these applies no matter what filter you then apply over the top. 

I will never get bored of the phone’s black and white mode.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
Don’t want black and white? No problem, the phone has plenty of color options for you.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Confused? Yeah, I’m not entirely surprised, there are a lot of variables at play when taking an image with this thing but it didn’t take me long to figure out how to get the look that I wanted. And let’s be honest, there aren’t many photographers who want fewer options in how to take a photo. 

Then there’s Essential Moment, which is its own standalone mode where you can select from three distinct styles: a black and white mode, “modern vintage,” or “Iconic CCD.” Each of these is designed to replicate specific looks from cameras of the past, and Xiaomi says it uses AI to analyze the scene to authentically reproduce color tones, vintage lens effects and film grain (though crucially not generative AI to actually alter anything in the scene). 

I used the Essential Moment mode here and I love the colors it’s produced.Andrew Lanxon/CNET
And the Essential Moment’s black and white mode has captured this curious pigeon magnificently.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I actually love this, especially the black and white option, which produces monochrome images with beautiful contrast and genuinely authentic-looking film grain. It’s the mode I’d end up using most often, I’m sure, and I’ve taken a bunch of photos with it that I really like. 

Oh, and that tiny ultrawide camera, weirdly separated from its friends? It’s not great, with nighttime shots being particularly disappointing here. On the upside, the main camera’s standard focal length is 23mm, which is already pretty wide, so you probably won’t miss the ultrawide much.

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: Processor, software and privacy display

While the base 18 Pro uses Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, the Pro Max ups the ante with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. It’s no surprise that the Pro Max is a seriously powerful bit of kit, returning benchmark scores up there with the powerhouse Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Everything ran exceptionally smoothly, from playing demanding 3D games like Genshin Impact to editing photos or navigating the Android 17 interface. I found much the same with the 18 Pro, too — I didn’t see a noticeable difference in performance.

I don’t mind Xiaomi’s software skin, as it’s easy enough for anyone familiar with Android to get to grips with. What I don’t like, though, is the company’s insistence on preloading it with an armada of apps including AliExpress, Netflix, WPS Office, TikTok and others. Together with the variety of Xiaomi apps also on board, the phone feels somewhat cluttered before you’ve even had a chance to add anything of your own. I’ve seen worse examples (Oppo has been bad with this), but it still irks me that the phone ends up feeling almost like it’s ad-supported. And if it is, surely it should be cheaper?

The rear screen has various useful features but it can also just show the clock and a cute cartoon animal. So that’s nice.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The display has a “privacy mode” that uses hardware dimming to limit how much of the screen can be seen by people peeping over your shoulder. It’s similar to the tech we saw earlier this year on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, although having seen them both side by side, Samsung’s seems better. On the S26 Ultra, the privacy boost means that, when viewed off angle, content becomes essentially invisible. On the Xiaomi, while it looked much dimmer from the sides, I could still make out words on screen. 

It helps a bit, sure, but it won’t block those creeps entirely. My advice is: if you’ve got information so sensitive that even a glimpse would be career-ending, maybe wait until you’re alone before you put it on screen.

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: Battery life and charging

The 7,050-mAh silicon-carbon battery in the larger Pro Max packs a punch, putting in some solid scores on our demanding battery rundown tests. After one hour of YouTube streaming, it dropped to 97%, then to 89% after the third hour. That puts it above the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, although still below the current champion, the iPhone 18 Pro Max. 

The deep red color of the phone looks great and the all-metal construction feels very premium to hold.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

In everyday use, you won’t struggle to get through a full day of mixed use and you can likely be quite demanding with it and still not worry about it conking out mid-afternoon. Take photos, watch videos, listen to music – don’t stress over it; this thing should hold out fine. 

The phone supports up to 100-watt wired fast charging, though you’ll need a Xiaomi fast charger to achieve the fastest speeds. I don’t have a Xiaomi charger (and the fastest it sells in the UK is 90W for £25), but I tried it with multiple third-party 100-watt chargers and the maximum I could get was around 65 watts. Even so, it went from 1% to 65% in 30 minutes of charging, which is still pretty quick — on par with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, in fact. Still, it should be able to go faster; you’ll just need to source a charger that will allow it. 

With its smaller 6,000-mAh battery the Xiaomi 18 Pro didn’t fare as well on our battery drain tests (it dropped to 93% after an hour of YouTube streaming) but in general use you’ll still comfortably get through most of a day on a single charge.

It’s a great all-round Android phone.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: Should you buy it? 

If you’re in the US, it’s something of a moot point. You can’t buy it. Sorry. Sure, you can probably import it from some third-party resellers, but it’s not officially on sale. 

If you’re somewhere where you can buy it, then lucky you — this phone is a blast. It ticks many of the boxes I’d expect from a flagship phone right now (camera quality in particular), and that second rear screen is the cherry on top. I expected it to feel like a pointless gimmick, and maybe it is a bit of a novelty, but it’s fun and I’ve already found it genuinely useful. 

I don’t like that there are so many hardware differences between the two phone sizes, as it forces you to have a much bigger model if you want the best performance. I prefer Apple’s approach: With the iPhone 18 Pro, I can have the same exact potent camera setup and processor performance, no matter which size I choose. With Xiaomi’s phones I’m forced to compromise between performance and pocketability. If you want the best camera, then go for the bigger model. Battery life is better, too.

title: Former Apple chairman Arthur Levinson files to sell $31.8 million in company stock
snippet: Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

Arthur Levinson’s stock sales are not unusual

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the company’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the company.

Today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his plans to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he currently holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

The filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

According to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

title: Apple hears Liquid Glass feedback, tests small but welcome change
snippet: Liquid Glass was one of the most controversial and polarizing UI changes Apple has made for a long time. The company listened to the feedback and made a number of changes, the most significant of which was to introduce a sliding transparency scale. Apple is currently testing a change some will consider insignificant but I personally find very welcome: softer edges when scrolling … more…
fullText:
Liquid Glass was one of the most controversial and polarizing UI changes Apple has made for a long time. The company listened to the feedback and made a number of changes, the most significant of which was to introduce a sliding transparency scale.

Apple is currently testing a change some will consider insignificant but I personally find very welcome: softer edges when scrolling … 

Apple’s introduction of the Liquid Glass UI split the Apple community, some hailing it as one of the best improvements seen for many years, and others rejecting it as a usability disaster.

As is often the case with any change, the controversy dampened significantly once people had a chance to get used to it. That is not the same as everyone being happy with it, however. Apple later tried to please most of the people most of the time with a slider that allows people to customize the level of transparency, from a very frosted glass look to an almost completely clear one.

Code sleuth pdfu has spotted that the company is currently testing a small but welcome additional choice.

They heard the feedback: Apple is testing the return of iOS 26’s softer scroll-edge effect in navigation bars when glass tint is set to 25% or lower.

Currently disabled behind UIKit/clear_glass_soft_pocket. Applies to the default/auto style. pic.twitter.com/D2NvKfESYa

— pdfu (@itspdfu) November 16, 2026

The difference is somewhat subtle, and some may consider it irrelevant, but as someone who has transparency maxed-out I’m a fan of the softer fade and would welcome the option to be able to reinstate this.

title: I’d rather use Android XR glasses over Meta Ray-Bans for the app alone
snippet: In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans. more…
fullText:
In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.

One of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration. It’s something we see frequently, and perhaps most well-known on smartwatches.

The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple. While we can’t show you the full app just yet as the one we were able to try was not completely final, it’s a very simple experience.

The app opens to an overview of your glasses to show their connection and battery status, with settings below for Gemini, apps, the camera, and more. You’ll also be able to see things such as what the various lights on the glasses mean, tutorials, and more. There’s no bloat and no messing around – it’s a utility to just make adjustments or control the glasses as needed.

	

You’ll probably be using this app mostly to view the photos and videos captured on Android XR glasses. Google has this set up to auto-import photos in nearly real-time. It only takes about 4 seconds to import and the process starts immediately for photos. Videos, on the other hand, take longer and may need to be manually imported (for the sake of battery in part, Google mentioned). 

Across the three main platforms, there are some differences. The iPhone app doesn’t import photos quite as fast, and Samsung has its own app to fit in with One UI’s design language for Galaxy users, but the core premise is the same across all three.

While we’ll have to see how this works in real life, I was blown away by how simple it all was, though that might be because the bar is below the floor.

Meta’s Ray-Bans (and newer Meta Glasses) dominate the smart glasses conversation, and I think that the app is one of the biggest problems. It’s certainly one of the biggest reasons I’ve barely touched my Wayfarers in recent months. That’s because, in early 2025, Meta replaced its dedicated “View” app for its glasses with a Meta AI app, which is just invasive and distasteful in my book. Meta is no stranger to shoving AI down the throat of its existing users. Another well-known move was converting Facebook and Instagram search into AI search boxes with creepy levels of context and invasive actions – it makes Google’s AI Overviews look tame by comparison. But I’d argue the most aggressive was this move with its glasses. Something as simple as tweaking a setting or importing a photo now forces you to dodge an AI chatbot. 

Truly, Meta’s app is the worst, and I applaud Google for building a very simple utility for Android XR glasses instead.

title: Google Wallet rolling out digital Google Home keys with supported locks on Android
snippet: Google Wallet for Android is rolling out support for digital home keys if you have a compatible smart lock in Google Home. more…
fullText:
Google Wallet for Android is rolling out support for digital home keys if you have a compatible smart lock in Google Home.

After adding a home key to Google Wallet, you can Tap to Unlock with your phone. This leverages NFC and “works even when your phone screen is locked” by default. However, you can adjust verification settings in the Google Wallet app to require screen lock or biometric authentication. This requires Android 9+.

There’s also support for Unlock on Approach with an Aliro Ultra Wideband (UWB)-compatible Android phone (see below) and an Aliro UWB-compatible lock. Wear OS watches are not supported at launch.

Google Pixel 10 Pro series and above

Select UWB-enabled Samsung Galaxy phones

Behind the scenes, the digital key is linked to the Google Home app rather than a single lock. As such, “each of your compatible Aliro locks will work with a single key in your Google Wallet.” Keys are added to Google Wallet using the Home app, which will prompt you to save after setup. You can also go to Home settings > Google Wallet key.

	
	

Afterward, your key “automatically syncs across compatible Android phones signed into your Google Wallet account.”

The card in Google Wallet features a simple Google Home logo with your home’s name in the top-right corner. 

The following locks are supported at launch: Aqara u400 (UWB and NFC), Schlage Sense Pro (NFC at launch and UWB to follow), and Nuki Keypad 2 NFC. Support for more models is coming.

Additionally, support is rolling out first to the Google Home Public Preview before coming to all users “over the coming weeks.”

title: You can now play Henry Cavill’s ‘Mustache Protocol’ game made on Googlebook [U]
snippet: As teased before the launch, Henry Cavill has built a video game on Googlebook, and it’s called Mustache Protocol. more…
fullText:
As teased before the launch, Henry Cavill has built a video game on Googlebook, and it’s called Mustache Protocol.

Update 11/11: “Mustache Protocol” is now available to play: googlebook.google/henry-cavill.

This 16-bit retro game has three levels and can be played on desktop or mobile. There are “hilarious power-ups and Easter eggs” throughout.

In honor of Movember, your gameplay supports men’s health. From November 11 to 30, for every game played, Google will donate $11 to Movember, up to $500,000. Every play helps drive awareness and funding for men’s mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer.

Original 11/4: Fully embracing the Mission: Impossible – Fallout meme, this 16-bit video game is “about stopping rogue CGI artists from erasing every mustache on the planet.”

	
	

Part of the new platform’s promotional push heading into the holiday season, Google’s announcement says the actor:

“…used Rambler on his Googlebook to organize his thoughts as he brainstormed.”

“…mocked up different aesthetics, added accessories, and fine-tuned the design with Magic Pointer, which let him select and combine visual elements on screen.”

“…was able to move from his Android phone to his Googlebook and back without losing context or interrupting his creative flow” with Continue On

It looks like Cavill used Google Antigravity and other AI tools on the HP Googlebook 14 to “translate natural language prompts into working 16-bit game mechanics.”

The game is not yet available. When it launches, Google will “donate $11 for every play during the month of November” as part of a partnership with Movember. The company will donate up to $500,000 to “help support awareness and funding for men’s mental health, suicide prevention, prostate cancer, and testicular cancer.”

Until then, you can watch a three-part series that details how “Henry designed the hero character, vibe coded meme-inspired superpowers, and added to the game’s soundtrack.”

title: MacBook Neo 2: Here’s everything we know so far
snippet: Apple released the all-new MacBook Neo earlier this year, and it’s been a resounding success by all indications. Here’s everything we know so far about what’s next for Apple’s most affordable laptop … more…
fullText:
Apple released the all-new MacBook Neo earlier this year, and it’s been a resounding success by all indications. Here’s everything we know so far about what’s next for Apple’s most affordable laptop …

MacBook Neo 2 features

A19 Pro chip

The current MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip, which is the same chip used in the iPhone 16 Pro. As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is working on a next-generation MacBook Neo powered by the A19 Pro chip.

In terms of performance, the A19 Pro is about 10-15% faster than the A18 Pro in single-core and multi-core CPU tests. The jump in GPU performance is even bigger, with benchmarks showing an up to 40% boost for the A19 Pro. This is because every GPU core in the A19 Pro has Neural Accelerators built in.

The A19 Pro chip is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone Air.

According to reporter Tim Culpan, Apple will likely use a “binned” version of the A19 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo. While the A19 Pro chip in the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6-core GPU, the MacBook Neo version of the chip will likely have a 5-core GPU.

More memory

One of the compromises of the MacBook Neo is that it has 8GB of RAM. The rest of Apple’s Mac lineup nowadays starts with 16GB of RAM.

The next-generation MacBook Neo won’t jump all the way to 16GB of RAM. Instead, it’s expected to offer 12GB of RAM thanks to the aforementioned A19 Pro.

As I wrote in my review, I don’t think it’s a huge limitation that the MacBook Neo has just 8GB of RAM. Still, an increase for the next-generation model is a great improvement.

New AI features

The combination of the A19 Pro chip and 12GB of RAM upgrades should also unlock support for Apple’s more powerful on-device AI model announced at WWDC. This model enables a more accurate dictation experience and new options for customizing the Siri voice.

The current MacBook Neo doesn’t support this feature because of its A18 Pro chip and 8GB of RAM.

New colors

The MacBook Neo is available in an array of fun colors, including citrus, blush, indigo, and silver. Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plan is to “periodically” update the MacBook Neo with new colors.

There aren’t any details on which colors the next-generation MacBook Neo will be available in.

MacBook Neo 2: Release date and wrap up

Apple released the current MacBook Neo in March. Tim Culpan reports that the A19 Pro version of the machine is slated for a release sometime in 2027.

What changes do you want Apple to make with the second-generation MacBook Neo? Are you a MacBook Neo user? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Dbrand’s new Fitbit Air band launches as the first official third-party strap
snippet: Dbrand says it was tasked with developing another strap option for the Fitbit Air; thus, the rugged and modern Pulse band was born. more…
fullText:
Dbrand says it was tasked with developing another strap option for the Fitbit Air; thus, the rugged and modern Pulse band was born.

Google has a small collection of official accessory partners it works with to create third-party add-ons for its products under the “Made for Google” umbrella. Dbrand happens to be one of them, and has been since the launch of the Pixel 7.

Available starting today, the Dbrand Pulse band launches for the Fitbit Air starting at $34.95. It’s the first official Made for Google strap that fits the Fitbit Air. It comes in two sizes and one color – black. It’s definitely a more rugged option, but having worn a pre-production unit for a couple of months, I can safely say it’s the most comfortable Fitbit Air band I’ve worn.

It’s constructed of sweat-resistant silicone with molded channels to let air in. It certainly looks like a heavy-duty band, which is perfect for a wearable made to go with you wherever.

	

We’ve expressed our frustrations with Google’s selection of straps before, but this is the first sign of Google looking to other partners to develop more options. Dbrand claims Google tasked them with developing a new band because the Fitbit Air has been such a major success. Hopefully, we see more Made for Google brands release bands for the Fitbit Air. This is a great first step.

Dbrand’s Pulse band for the Fitbit Air is available on the company’s website, starting today.

title: iOS 27.3 brings vertical video and video podcasts to Apple TV app
snippet: iOS 27.3 beta 2 debuted today and includes two new types of video in the Apple TV app: vertical ‘clips’ and video podcasts. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 beta 2 debuted today and includes two new types of video in the Apple TV app: vertical ‘clips’ and video podcasts.

Apple TV app now features short-form vertical video, plus video shows from Apple Podcasts

The Apple TV app is expanding in two key ways with iOS 27.3, which is now in beta and ships next month.

First, Apple is introducing vertical video through a new ‘clips’ feature.

Similar to what streaming services like Netflix and Disney+ offer, the feature is a way to let users sample short-form previews of Apple TV content in a TikTok-style interface.

Inside the TV app in iOS 27.3, the Home tab has a new section: ‘Explore Clip Collections.’ Currently the collections include themed titles like ‘Absolute Adrenaline,’ ‘Animal Action,’ ‘Close Calls,’ and ‘Mind-Bending Moments.’

Tap to open a collection and you’ll start playing a short-form clip from Apple Originals with the option to swipe vertically to watch other clips. As you’d expect, Apple provides convenient buttons for adding the TV show or movie to your Watchlist.

iOS 27.3 also brings video podcasts from the Apple Podcasts app into TV.

As we reported this morning, there’s a dedicated video podcasts section coming to the TV app. But you can also, via your Account Settings, choose to sync playback data from Apple Podcasts.

If you enable sync, then video podcasts played in one app will be added to the queue and playback history in both apps.

What do you think of the latest TV app changes in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

title: Pixel Journal update rolls out Recorder integration, file export [U]
snippet: Following the last update in August, Google is rolling out a sizable update to Pixel Journal that adds Recorder audio entries and file exports. more…
fullText:
Following the last update in August, Google is rolling out a sizable update to Pixel Journal that adds Recorder audio entries and file exports.

Update 11/16: Updates for Pixel Journal (version 2026.10.27.x) and Pixel Recorder (4.2.20261001.x) are widely rolling out. After installing (be sure to open the apps and Force stop), you’ll see “Record new audio” and “Add existing recording” in the Add item menu. 

The first option directly launches the Recorder app into a new session, while the second brings up a list of previous recordings. The Journal app will show an inline audio player and transcript, which can be removed.

Curiously, these updates weren’t mentioned as part of the November 2026 Pixel Drop.

	

Journal November 2026 updates:

• Recorder integration: Record new audio or add existing recordings from Pixel Recorder, complete with playable clips and transcripts

• Journal export: Export your entries and media to view offline anytime

Original 11/10: From the “Add item” plus menu in entries, you’ll see “Record new audio” join the existing Take photo/video, Add photo, Health Connect activity, and location & map options.

At the moment, this audio integration is not live as Pixel Recorder also requires an update that we’re not seeing in the Play Store yet.

Being able to add a “voice entry with audio” is a pretty common feature for journaling apps. A transcription capability looks to be available for Google’s implementation.

Meanwhile, in Pixel Journal settings, there’s a new “Export your journal” option. This creates a ZIP file of all your entries, including images. Text is exported as HTML files. 

Version 2026.10.27.x of Pixel Journal is still rolling out via Google Play today.

title: Here’s a HomeView feature that should come to every Apple device
snippet: This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode. more…
fullText:
This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode.

On iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time. While this is generally helpful and certainly appreciated, it isn’t super granular. Of course, you can adjust the time when it switches, but generally speaking its just a one time toggle.

HomeView offers a new dark mode option

With HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode. In display settings, once you enable automatic dark mode, there’s the usual two settings you’d see on other Apple platforms: sunrise to sunset, as well as a custom schedule. HomeView takes it a step further with ambient mode, where the ambient light sensor determines whether or not you should be in light or dark mode.

Of course, a sunrise to sunset schedule generally works for most cases. However, if you’re up late at night with your lights turned on, you still might prefer light mode in an instance where macOS would generally be in dark mode. Similarly, if you wake up later in the day with your curtains shut, at say 11am, you might not want to immediately see light mode on your phone the second you open your eyes.

There are tons of good reasons for why someone would prefer ambient light-based automatic light and dark mode switching. HomeView software is the first Apple platform to enable this, and I’d love to see it come to iPhone, iPad, and Mac starting next year with OS 28.

Apple’s Messages app is the most-used app for many iPhone users. As such, Apple regularly makes the app better with new features and important changes. Here’s a rundown of some of Apple’s biggest recent changes to Messages on iPhone.

My favorite new features in Messages

With iOS 26 last year, Apple added a host of new features to Messages. Here are some of my favorites:

Message backgrounds: you can now set custom backgrounds for your individual threads and group chats in Messages. This gives you a new way to customize your conversations.

Group chat upgrades: Apple added some much-needed improvements to group chats in Messages, including typing indicators. Group chats also support Apple Cash, making it easier to split a bill.

Polls: When it comes time to decide where to go for dinner, what time to meet up, or anything else, you can now create polls in the Messages app. On Apple Intelligence devices, the Messages app can also automatically suggest and create polls for you.

New filtering options: Spam messages are an increasingly big problem for iPhone users. In the upper-right corner of the Messages app, you can filter messages based on Unknown Senders, Transactions, Promotions, and Spam. This makes it easier to keep your main Messages interface clutter-free.

With iOS 27 this year, Apple added even more to the Messages app — headlined by a focus on bug fixes and performance improvements.

Bug fixes: Apple has fixed three of the most annoying Messages bugs. Failed messages will automatically retry sending, there’s now support for continuous sending of photos, videos, and messages, and improved syncing across devices. These changes alone make for a huge quality-of-life improvement for Messages.

One-tap suggestions: In iOS 27, the Messages app offers one-tap suggestions based on the context of your messages, such as creating a reminder or a note.

Smart reply: The Messages app in iOS 27 now offers much more intelligent Smart Reply suggestions that are based on your personalized writing styles.

All of this comes as Apple has also continued to improve its implementation of RCS, making cross-platform communication with your Android friends and family even better. Most notably, Apple this year added support for end-to-end encryption when using RCS.

What are some of your favorite features in the Messages app? What’s on your wishlist? Let us know down in the comments.

title: November 2026 Pixel Drop: Create My Widget, HiLight for Google Messages, Pixel 10 Rambler, & more
snippet: Like last year, the next Pixel Drop is rolling out a month early in November. Coupled with Android 17 QPR2, it’s quite a big Feature Drop for Gemini and other AI capabilities, as well as the Pixel 10 series. more…
fullText:
Like last year, the next Pixel Drop is rolling out a month early in November. Coupled with Android 17 QPR2, it’s quite a big Feature Drop for Gemini and other AI capabilities, as well as the Pixel 10 series.

Pixel Watch Drop: Create My Widget, Phone-to-Watch Unlock, and Wear OS 7.1

Gemini Intelligence is coming to the Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, and Pixel 10 Pro Fold. The lead feature is Rambler to automatically remove filler words and format your transcription.

The Pixel 10 series also gets Gemini app automation for ordering groceries, ride-sharing, meal delivery, marketplace transactions, and booking reservations. Proactive Gemini Actions let you “send groceries right to your Google Keep list straight from ongoing conversations” and more.

	

The Pixel 11 and 10 are getting Create My Widget. This generative UI capability lets you create custom homescreen objects using natural language. For example, you can create a sports widget or an event countdown. The feature first debuted on Googlebooks.

On the Pixel 11, Gemini Call Screen is an “intelligent, proactive assistant that screens incoming inquiries on demand.” Replacing Manual Call Screen, Gemini will speak to callers in a more conversational manner than before.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 10+ now lets Gemini make calls on your behalf in the US. Use cases include changing reservations, putting items on hold, and checking inventory. Beta testing started in September.

The AI features continue with 10 new Custom Icon styles. Following the March introduction, Google has upgraded the experience with Nano Banana for higher-quality icons. Available on Pixel 6a+.

Pixel Solver in the Google Calculator app provides generative AI custom templates and allows for conversational, multi-step problem solving using prompts. This is available on Pixel 11+.

Unit Conversion is a “top-tier module” that saves you from switching between your browser and the Calculator app. It offers inline mathematics, combined unit interpretation, and real-time exchange rates on the Pixel 6a+.

On the Pixel 11 Pro, Pro XL, and Pro Fold, HiLight now supports Google Messages notifications after being restricted to phone calls and Gemini at launch. 

Pixel Search is now available on the Pixel 6 and newer to provide a more integrated on-device lookup experience that spans apps, web, settings, and other personal content. It allows for natural language search from the search bar at the top of the app grid. 

	

Extreme Battery Charging is now available on the Pixel 10 series.

Following the 2.0 redesign in September, Pixel VIPs now supports Live Location Sharing. This will surface real-time information and battery status from Find Hub in contact cards and homescreen widgets on the Pixel 6a+. 

Transit Mode has been upgraded to automatically trigger based on device sensors. This is available on the Pixel 6a+.

International feature expansions today include:

Notification Summaries are now available in Germany, Canada, France, Spain, Italy, India, and Taiwan on Pixel 9+.

Similarly, Notification Organizer is now available in German and Japanese.
